extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in research integrity (researchers, science journalists, whistleblowers, and students)
extracted.subtask_description: An 'About' blog page and reader discussion for Retraction Watch describing the author's background and collecting comments about retractions, reproducibility, authorship ethics, and related practices in scientific publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducible research: data, methods, clear path
rubrics_metrics.description: Reproducible research means: 1) data well defined; 2) methods expressed in a way to be redone; 3) papers with a clear path from data to results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure datasets are described and accessible (as allowed), provide methodological detail sufficient for replication, and make the analytical path from raw data to reported results explicit. This is presented as the minimal set of requirements for reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship transparency and compliance with journal/practice guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Ghost-writing is not ethical: contributors who write or substantially revise manuscripts should be named (as authors or in Acknowledgments) and their roles specified; work that meets a journal's authorship definition must result in being named as an author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow established guidelines (CSE, WAME, COPE, ICMJE) and professional associations for medical writers (AMWA, EMWA). Check and follow a journal's Instructions for Authors to determine when contribution warrants authorship versus acknowledgment. Explicitly document contributors' roles to avoid disputes and potential charges of ghost authorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction notices should be informative (avoid opaque notices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Retraction notices that provide almost no explanation are problematic; notices should explain the reason(s) for retraction rather than give minimal or opaque text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When retracting work, journals and authors should describe the cause (error, misconduct, duplication, inability to reproduce, etc.), who requested/recommended the retraction, and any implications for the findings. Clear notices help the community understand the issue and prevent further propagation of invalid results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain primary data and records
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers should keep primary data and records so they can demonstrate the integrity of their work if questioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain organized, accessible primary data, lab notes, and analysis records for the period required by your field/institution. Retention facilitates investigations, defends against erroneous accusations, and supports reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report questionable or suspect publications to appropriate venues
rubrics_metrics.description: Questionable published articles should be reported to journals, platforms like PubPeer, or databases such as Retraction Watch so concerns can be investigated and publicized appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use established channels (journal editorial offices, PubPeer, Retraction Watch tip lines) and provide specific evidence (data, figure comparisons, methods concerns). Follow each venue's submission/reporting guidance and preserve communications and documentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify and document misconduct cases for analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: If building a database of frauds, classify incidents by attributes such as: a) number of distinct actions, b) number of persons involved, c) papers produced, d) citations of those papers, e) consequences/actions taken, f) how the fraud was discovered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect structured metadata for each case to enable statistical study and trend analysis (e.g., scope, methods of detection, institutional responses). This supports better understanding of causes and preventative measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reuse/duplication of figures without attribution and check copyright
rubrics_metrics.description: Reusing figures (or duplicating images) without clear attribution or permission can be construed as duplication, misconduct, or copyright violation and may prompt retraction or editorial action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reusing a methodological or illustrative figure, clearly attribute the source and obtain permission if required. Distinguish example/methodological images from data and make their provenance explicit to readers and editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disseminate corrections/retractions broadly via free databases
rubrics_metrics.description: Medical corrections and retractions should be reported to widely accessible, mostly free databases (e.g., PLOS-hosted resources) so lay readers and practitioners can access corrected information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In addition to journal retraction notices, share retraction/correction metadata with open repositories and databases (and consider notifying aggregators like Cochrane where relevant) to maximize discoverability and public health benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journals should avoid citation-manipulation practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Practices that game citation indices (e.g., pressuring authors to add citations to the journal to boost impact factor) are problematic and have led to investigations and retractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and publishers should prohibit coercive citation practices, be transparent about editorial policies, and ensure peer review and editorial decisions are independent of citation-inflation incentives.
